title: Fallacy of the Single Cause
hook: The neatest explanation is often the one that cut away the machinery.
counterintuition: A single cause feels useful because it is clean; map the interacting causes before the story starts choosing for you.
keyTakeaway: Single-cause stories make decisions feel clear while hiding the mechanism. Build a small cause map before assigning blame, credit, or action.

breakdown.fastRead: The triage desk blames a rise in patient dropouts on one rude intake clerk. Desmond can fire the clerk and feel decisive. Instead, he marks single cause on the dropout table and adds wait time, parking, referral wording, and evening staffing. The clerk may matter, but the mechanism is wider. A clean explanation can be a dirty map. The fallacy is not looking for causes. It is stopping at the first cause that makes the room feel finished.
breakdown.deepRead:
The fallacy of the single cause starts with a relief: now we know why it happened. One villain, one policy, one market shock, one bad hire, one clever feature. The explanation fits in a sentence, which makes it easy to repeat and easy to defend.

Real outcomes usually have joints. A seafood bid may fail because the cold-storage price rose, the export window moved, the buyer changed inspection rules, and the team assumed the old shipping rhythm still held. Any one factor can be true. None has to be the whole cause.

Single cause is comfort wearing a lab coat.

The correction is a mechanism map, not a lecture about complexity. Put the suspected cause in the center. Add two enabling conditions, one missing restraint, and one alternative path that could produce the same result. Then ask which lever the next decision can actually move. Multi-causality is useful only when it changes the choice in front of you.

A fintech review shows the difference. Evelyn sees a default model fail and hears the room blame one new variable. The maintenance key on the table belongs to the office server rack, and she uses it as a prop: one key does not open every lock. Before approving the rollback, she maps stale income data, a changed fraud rule, a vendor delay, and borrower seasonality. The rollback becomes narrower, faster, and less theatrical.
breakdown.fullRead:
The port scheduling office smells of wet rope and old printer toner. Bethany watches a storm track crawl across the screen while a dispatcher says the missed sailings were caused by one cautious supervisor. The claim is tempting because it gives the port a person to correct. Bethany writes Tolstoy in the margin, then draws arrows from wind timing, tug availability, crew-hour limits, and the new customs inspection window. The next choice changes: she revises the schedule rule instead of disciplining one supervisor.

The fallacy of the single cause does not mean one cause is never important. Sometimes one fuse really did blow. Sometimes one contract clause, one wrong dose, or one broken pipe deserves urgent attention. The error is treating a clean explanation as proof that the other parts of the mechanism can be ignored.

What else had to be true for this cause to matter?

War and Peace keeps returning to the same pressure: great events do not move because one person pulls one lever. Tolstoy's battle scenes make single-cause history look too tidy for human systems. Commanders give orders, soldiers misunderstand, mud slows movement, fear changes timing, and later a story turns the mess into one clean cause. Christopher Chabris and Daniel Simons use that kind of intuition failure to show how easily a vivid explanation can crowd out the unseen network behind it.

A school literacy case has the same shape in smaller form. Moira sees a reading intervention miss its target, and the clean explanation is that parents did not practice at home. The booking ledger shows another pattern: substitute teachers, late bus arrivals, testing-week interruptions, and a change in library hours all hit the same group. Parent practice still belongs on the map. It no longer gets to carry the whole failure alone.

The mechanism map should change the next choice, not decorate the old one.

The limited bakery batch gives a softer example. Glenn's almond loaves sell out by 10:30 a.m., and the grant rubric for a small-business award praises scarcity as the cause. In the postmortem, he adds rain that pushed commuters indoors, a nearby conference break, a social post from a local critic, and a smaller batch size after a flour delivery problem. Scarcity helped. It was not the engine by itself. The next batch plan changes because the cause map changed.

The practical test is simple. If your explanation names one cause, ask whether it is a trigger, an enabling condition, a background pressure, or a story-friendly symbol. A trigger starts motion. An enabling condition lets it matter. A background pressure raises the odds. A symbol makes people nod. Confusing these roles creates bad action: firing a person when a process failed, copying a tactic when timing did the work, or blaming culture when incentives and constraints made the behavior rational.

The limit is that maps can become fog. You do not need twenty arrows before deciding. You need enough causes to stop the first neat story from pretending to be the mechanism. For a small choice, add two other causes. For a high-stakes choice, add the sequence: trigger, conditions, constraints, and feedback loop. Then decide from the map you can defend.

examples.title: Desmond widens the dropout table
examples.scenario: The dropout table sits under a triage monitor in a Halifax emergency desk at 8:40 p.m. Desmond, the shift lead, must decide whether one rude clerk caused the lost patients. He writes single cause on the table, adds wait time and referral wording, and changes the action from firing to a process review.
examples.whatToDo: Add enabling conditions and alternative paths before assigning one cause.
examples.whyItMatters: The clerk may matter, but firing one person will miss the mechanism if waits, wording, and staffing made the dropouts likely.

planSpec.domain: a hospital triage desk applying Fallacy of the Single Cause under operational pressure

examples.title: Allison maps the failed export bid
examples.scenario: "The warehouse quote killed the deal," the broker says in a St. John's seafood office at 6:10 a.m. Allison, the export manager, must decide whether to switch cold-storage vendors. She marks multi-causality on an organ-donor form, adds inspection timing and buyer credit terms, and changes the bid review.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the visible cost from the other conditions that made the bid fail.
examples.whyItMatters: A higher storage quote can be real without being the only cause. The next bid needs the whole chain.

examples.whyItMatters: The supervisor's caution may be part of the story, but the decision improves only when the surrounding causes are visible.

In a Leeds school office at 3:50 p.m., she must decide whether to blame parents. She marks clean explanation on the booking ledger, adds substitutes and library hours, and changes the intervention.
examples.whatToDo: Add the timing and constraints that make a clean blame story incomplete.
examples.whyItMatters: Parent practice may matter, but the intervention fails differently if transport, staffing, and access are also causes.

examples.title: Glenn rewrites the batch postmortem
examples.scenario: Why did the almond loaves vanish before the lunch rush when last week's batch sat untouched? Glenn reviews the Manchester bakery postmortem at 11:05 a.m. with a grant rubric beside the register. He marks fallacy, adds rain, a conference break, and batch size, then changes the next bake plan.
examples.whatToDo: Explain the sellout with several causes before scaling the batch.
examples.whyItMatters: Scarcity may help sales, but copying it alone ignores traffic, weather, publicity, and production limits.

questions.prompt: In a fallacy-single case, a hospital team says patient complaints rose because one new receptionist has a sharp tone, the same month added a new intake form, longer parking walks, and fewer evening nurses. What is the fallacy of the single cause?
choices: Treating the receptionist as the whole explanation before mapping the other causes.
Rose receptionist sharp makes fallacy-single hospital team look credible; use says patient complaints first and revisit tone month added when intake form longer shifts.
Longer parking walks supports a narrower read of complaints rose receptionist; keep sharp tone month central and leave added intake form aside.
questions.explanation: The receptionist may matter, but the error is letting one cause absorb the form, parking, and staffing changes.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause makes fallacy-single case feel more decisive than the record supports, and that misprices hospital team in this scene. The correct move keepss the choice by treating the receptionist as the whole explanation before mapping the.

questions.prompt: During a fallacy-single review, a seafood exporter loses a bid and blames the cold-storage quote, the buyer also shortened the inspection window, changed credit terms, and ordered less volume. What should the manager do before switching vendors?
choices: Fallacy-single seafood exporter looks strong enough to guide loses blames cold-storage; quote buyer also can wait unless shortened inspection window changes the stakes.
Also shortened inspection gives a practical reason for cold-storage quote buyer; terms ordered less belongs after window changed credit clarifies the result.
Map storage cost, inspection timing, credit terms, and order volume before choosing a lever.
questions.explanation: The storage quote is only one piece. A cause map points to the lever that actually changes the next bid.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause works by letting fallacy-single seafood crowd out exporter loses, which can misreads the blames cold-storage decision. Map storage cost, inspection timing, credit terms, and order volume before choosing a lever keeps the practical cost tied.

questions.prompt: When fallacy-single pressure appears, a port director says one cautious supervisor caused three missed sailings. Logs show wind timing, tug shortages, customs delays, and crew-hour limits. Which action best breaks the single-cause story?
choices: Build a sequence showing how the supervisor's call interacted with weather, tugs, customs, and crew limits.
Delays crew-hour limits fits the immediate pressure around three missed sailings; hold cautious supervisor caused steady and test port director says later.
Appears port director looks strong enough to guide says cautious supervisor; caused three missed can wait unless sailings logs show changes the stakes.
questions.explanation: The best answer keeps the supervisor in the picture but adds the conditions that made the call produce missed sailings.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause turns appears port into a shortcut, so the room can overweights director says while missing cautious supervisor. Build a sequence showing how the supervisor's call interacted with weather, tugs, customs, and crew limits protects the.

questions.prompt: After fallacy-single risk surfaces, a model review blames a default spike on one new variable, the spike also follows stale income data, a changed fraud rule, and a vendor delay. What is the most useful next move?
choices: Vendor delay what points toward a quicker call on variable also follows; let blames default spike stand until changed fraud rule contradicts it.
Draw a mechanism map and test which cause or interaction the next release can change.
Surfaces model blames looks strong enough to guide default spike variable; also follows stale can wait unless income data changed changes the stakes.
questions.explanation: A mechanism map avoids both overreaction and paralysis. It finds which part of the causal chain the next release can move.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause would push the model blames case toward default spike, creating a cost when variable also stays untested. The useful guardrail is to draw a mechanism map and test which cause or interaction the next release.

questions.prompt: If fallacy-single reasoning takes over, a school blames weak reading scores on parents not practicing at home. Calendar notes show substitute coverage, bus delays, library closures, and testing-week disruptions. Which conclusion is strongest?
choices: Parent practice may be one cause, but the intervention plan should include the timing and access constraints.
Coverage delays library points toward a quicker call on reading scores parents; let school blames weak stand until notes show substitute contradicts it.
Library closures testing-week fits the immediate pressure around parents practicing home; hold weak reading scores steady and test reasoning school blames later.
questions.explanation: The parent-practice story becomes usable only after the other causes are added to the plan.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause converts blames weak into the loudest signal, which can rushes reading scores before parents practicing is checked. The better answer separatess attention on parent practice may be one cause, but the intervention plan should include.

questions.prompt: While fallacy-single pressure builds, a bakery owner says scarcity alone made a small batch sell out, the sellout happened during heavy rain, a nearby conference break, and a local critic's post. What should he do before doubling down on scarcity?
choices: Small batch sell makes builds bakery owner look credible; use says scarcity alone first and revisit sellout happened heavy when rain nearby conference shifts.
Sell sellout happened supports a narrower read of pressure builds bakery; keep owner says scarcity central and leave alone small batch aside.
Compare batch size with traffic, weather, publicity, and timing before changing production.
questions.explanation: Scarcity may help, but the next bake plan needs the interacting causes that created the sellout.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause hides inside the fallacy-single pressure choice because fallacy-single pressure seems sufficient, yet the cost lands in fallacy-single pressure. Compare batch size with traffic, weather, publicity, and timing before changing production brings the fallacy-single pressure comparison.

questions.prompt: Before the fallacy-single call, a nonprofit director says donations fell because the newsletter subject line was dull. The same week, a payment link broke for mobile users and a matching grant expired. What question best tests the explanation?
choices: Users matching grant points toward a quicker call on newsletter subject line; let says donations fell stand until link broke mobile contradicts it.
Grant expired what fits the immediate pressure around line dull week; hold fell newsletter subject steady and test director says donations later.
Which causes changed at the same time, and which one can the next campaign isolate or repair?
questions.explanation: The useful question maps simultaneous causes and turns them into testable levers. A better subject line alone may miss the broken link.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause pressures the call nonprofit decision toward the easy reading of call nonprofit. That can inflates the real cost unless the choice is grounded in which causes changed at the same time, and which one can.

questions.prompt: Turnover rises after remote work expands, and a retention lead blames damaged culture. Payroll records show a pay freeze, a new competitor hiring nearby, and a promotion backlog. What is wrong with the clean story?
choices: It treats culture as the single cause while ignoring incentives, labor market pressure, and career paths.
Work expands retention looks strong enough to guide lead blames damaged; culture payroll records can wait unless show freeze competitor changes the stakes.
Retention lead blames gives a practical reason for remote work expands; records show freeze belongs after damaged culture payroll clarifies the result.
questions.explanation: Remote work or culture may still matter, but the clean story hides other causes that affect turnover directly.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause is the mechanism here: one explanation hides interacting causes, so after remote can overpower after remote. It treats culture as the single cause while ignoring incentives, labor market pressure, and career paths keeps the scenario.

questions.prompt: Two fallacy-single signals compete: a city task force explains a crash increase by blaming one confusing sign. The same intersection had a new delivery zone, changed light timing, and more cyclists after a bridge closure. Which plan best handles the causal claim?
choices: Fallacy-single signals compete looks strong enough to guide city task force; explains crash increase can wait unless blaming confusing sign changes the stakes.
Map sign design, delivery blockage, light timing, and cyclist volume before choosing the first intervention.
Confusing sign intersection makes task force explains look credible; use crash increase blaming first and revisit delivery zone changed when light timing cyclists shifts.
questions.explanation: The sign may be a cause, but the task force should choose from the mapped mechanism, not from the neatest object to blame.
questions.whyItMatters: Fallacy of the Single Cause makes the city task evidence look cleaner than it is, risking a city task mistake in this setting. The answer protects city task by asking for map sign design, delivery blockage, light timing, and cyclist.

reviewCards.front: A room has one clean explanation for a messy result. What additional causes must be mapped?
reviewCards.back: Map multiple contributing causes and their links. One clean factor may be real while still being incomplete.

reviewCards.front: A cause feels obvious. What should go on the small map?
reviewCards.back: Add the suspected cause, two enabling conditions, one missing restraint, and one alternative path.

reviewCards.front: A person is being blamed for an outcome. What should you check?
reviewCards.back: Check which system conditions made that person's action matter before assigning the whole cause.

reviewCards.front: A tactic worked once and everyone names one reason. What is the risk?
reviewCards.back: The named reason may be only a trigger while timing, constraints, or background pressure did the work.

reviewCards.front: Your map has become too complex. What is enough for a live decision?
reviewCards.back: Add just enough causes to stop the first neat story from pretending to be the whole mechanism.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Replace one-cause stories with a small mechanism map before assigning blame, credit, or action.

ifThenPlans.plan: If one person is named as the cause, then I will list the conditions that made that action matter.
If one tactic gets all the credit, then I will add timing, constraints, and background pressure.
If a failure has a neat explanation, then I will map trigger, enabling condition, restraint, and feedback.
If a proposed fix targets one cause, then I will ask which other causes remain after the fix.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one explanation you heard today. Write the named cause, two enabling conditions, and one alternative path before repeating it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, turn one blame or credit story into a four-part mechanism map before deciding what to change.

tryThisNow: Pick one neat explanation you recently accepted. Add two enabling conditions and one alternative cause before you repeat it.

memorableLines.text: A clean explanation can be a dirty map.
Single cause is comfort wearing a lab coat.
The mechanism map should change the next choice, not decorate the old one.
